power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Abstraction is central to human cognition, yet the term covers at least three senses that are routinely conflated: abstractness (how far a concept is removed from perceptible experience), specificity (how general or inclusive a category is), and the process by which conceptual change.
We propose GEST-A (Grounded, Embodied, Situated Trajectories of Abstraction), a hierarchical and dynamic framework that separates these senses.

Being abstract is a concept's position in a dimensional space of grounding (physical-world constraints), embodiment (body-specific sensorimotor and interoceptive experience), and situatedness (dependence on context of use), with specificity as orthogonal descriptor.

Becoming abstract, in this view, is a trajectory through this space, driven by generalization and re-weighting of grounded, embodied, and situated content, and linked to a shift in feature structure from complete overlap to family resemblance.

Using number concepts to illustrate these dynamics, we position GEST-A against earlier hybrid accounts of grounding, clarify that linguistic labels are cues and binding devices rather than constituting concepts, and argue that abstract concepts constrain rather than refute embodied cognition.
We also revisit concreteness ratings and the symbol grounding problem, and derive testable predictions.
Abstract concepts reveal language as a powerful scaffold for building conceptual knowledge that exceeds individual sensorimotor experience.

The capacity to form abstract concepts, that is, to extract regularities across experiences and represent them independently of particular instances, is fundamental to human intellectual achievement (Barsalou, 2005; Dove, 2016).
text.formatted: The capacity to form abstract concepts, that is, to extract regularities across experiences and represent them independently of particular instances, is fundamental to human intellectual achievement <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Barsalou, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Dove, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: From mathematics to morality, from justice to jealousy, abstract concepts permeate thought and communication.
Yet, as with William James's remark about attention, everyone knows what abstraction is until asked to define it.

James himself pressed the difficulty from the other side: we ought to speak of "a feeling of and, a feeling of if, a feeling of but," as readily as of a feeling of blue or of cold (James, 1890, vol. 1, pp. 245-246).

text.text: Even the most abstract logical relations, on this view, have an experiential and situated character (see also Johnson, 2017, Chapter 2).

text.text: This insight anticipated the contemporary debate about whether, and how, abstract concepts are grounded in experience (Friedrich et al., 2025; Kiefer & Trumpp, 2026).
text.formatted: This insight anticipated the contemporary debate about whether, and how, abstract concepts are grounded in experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Friedrich et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Kiefer & Trumpp, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: That debate has been slowed by a terminological problem.

The word "abstract" is used in (at least) three different senses: It is used for abstractness, the degree to which a concept is removed from perceptible, sensorimotor experience (JUSTICE versus CANDY); for generality, the degree to which a category is inclusive rather than specific (FOOD versus CANDY; JUSTICE versus RESTORATIVE JUSTICE); and for abstraction, the process by which concepts are formed, generalized, and transformed.
These senses are related but not equivalent.
BANANA and FRUIT are both concrete yet differ strongly in specificity; FREEDOM and FREEDOM OF SPEECH are both abstract yet differ in specificity too (Bolognesi et al., 2020).

text.text: Conflating these senses has consequences: findings about "abstract concepts" may reflect either of these senses, and claims about conceptual grounding hold for one but not the other (Bolognesi, 2025).

text.text: This paper asks what a theory of abstract concepts must explain once these senses are separated, and develops a hierarchical and dynamic framework, GEST-A (Grounded, Embodied, Situated Trajectories of Abstraction), in response.

GEST-A builds on the TEST theory of cognition (Myachykov et al., 2014), on similar hierarchical views of numerical cognition (Fischer, 2012 (Fischer, , 2018 (Fischer, , 2024)), and on our earlier commentary in this journal, which proposed that abstractness has grounded, embodied, and situated aspects (Myachykov & Fischer, 2019) in response to the account of abstract concepts as words used as social tools (Borghi et al., 2019).

text.text: Several ingredients of our argument are not new.

Proposals that abstract concepts form a continuum rather than a dichotomy, that they are heterogeneous, that concreteness ratings are an imperfect measure, and that hybrid accounts combining grounded, linguistic, and intermediate representations are viable, all have a long history (Section 3).
The novel contribution we claim is more specific, and it has five parts: 1.
A separation of abstractness, specificity, and abstraction, with working definitions that can be mapped onto a recent consensus glossary (Reilly et al., 2025) (Section 2).

Terminology: Abstractness, abstraction, specificity, and the concept-word distinction 2.1 Abstractness, concreteness, and specificity A recent multidisciplinary consensus project defined "abstraction" as the process of forming general ideas or concepts by extracting similarities across instances, and separated it explicitly from "abstractness", a property of concepts or words (Reilly et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Terminology: Abstractness, abstraction, specificity, and the concept-word distinction 2.1 Abstractness, concreteness, and specificity A recent multidisciplinary consensus project defined "abstraction" as the process of forming general ideas or concepts by extracting similarities across instances, and separated it explicitly from "abstractness", a property of concepts or words <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Reilly et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The glossary also records principled views on how abstractness should be defined, which shows that the field has not converged.
We adopt this process-property distinction and use the terms as summarized in Box 1.
By abstractness we mean the degree to which a concept's content is detached from direct, perceptible, bodily experience.
It is graded, and we argue that it is expressed by three dimensions (Section 4).
Concreteness, as indexed by rating studies, is its conventional opposite and serves as an empirical proxy, not a definition.
Specificity (or its inverse, generality) refers to where a category sits in an inclusion hierarchy, that is, its semantic granularity.

The empirical decoupling of concreteness and specificity is now well documented. Bolognesi et al. (2020) operationalized and tested the relation between conceptual concreteness and categorical specificity and argued that they should be treated as separate. Muraki and Pexman (2026) have since published specificity norms for 8,500 English words, and Bolognesi (2025) argues that specificity is a missing piece in theories of embodied language comprehension.

text.text: From this, we draw two conclusions: First, ratings of concreteness and ratings of specificity measure different things, and a theory of abstract concepts must say which of them it addresses.

Second, embodiment is unlikely to be a unitary phenomenon, operating identically across conceptual categories: How a concept is grounded depends not only on perceptual accessibility but also on semantic granularity, and linguistic and other contextual constraints.
GEST-A is primarily a theory of abstractness and of the abstraction process that alters it.
It treats specificity as an orthogonal descriptor (Section 4.5).
We distinguish two sub-processes that the single word "abstraction" covers.
Generalization is the extraction of similarity across instances, accompanied by loss of specificity; this is the sense captured in Reilly et al.'s (2025) consensus glossary.
text.formatted: Generalization is the extraction of similarity across instances, accompanied by loss of specificity; this is the sense captured in <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Reilly et al.'s (2025)</ref> consensus glossary.

text.text: Detachment is the progressive re-weighting of grounded, embodied, and situated content through which a concept's abstractness increases.
The two can dissociate: FRUIT is more general than BANANA but not necessarily more abstract.
Conversely, a child's THREE, initially anchored in fingers and subitized arrays, can become a node in a relational number system (Section 6.5) without becoming more inclusive.
"Becoming abstract" in the present article refers to detachment, with generalization being one among several routes.
A second source of confusion concerns the relation between concepts and words.
We take a concept to be a mental representation of a category, kind, or relation that supports categorization, inference, and action, and that can in principle exist and operate without a word.
Three observations motivate this separation.
First, concepts exist outside language.
Preverbal infants and nonhuman animals categorize objects and discriminate quantities, and adults hold concepts for which they have no ready word.
Second, one lexical form can map onto several concepts.
MARS the planet, MARS the Roman god, and MARS the confectionery are distinct concepts that happen to share a form; they are not three instances of one concept.
Such polysemy and homonymy matter for how word-level ratings should be interpreted, but they are a lexical phenomenon and not evidence of contextual flexibility within a single concept.

Third, dissociations between number concepts and number words (for example, preserved exact calculation despite severe agrammatism; Varley et al., 2005) suggest that even the most language-dependent concepts are not identical to the words that name them.

text.text: What, then, is the role of language?
We distinguish three relations between a label and a concept.
As a cue, the label activates or constrains a concept in context (Lupyan & Lewis, 2019).
text.formatted: As a cue, the label activates or constrains a concept in context <ref type="bibr">(Lupyan & Lewis, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: As a binding device or placeholder, the label links instances that share no common perceptible feature during learning and maintenance, so that a coherent category can form and persist (Carey, 2009; Dobler et al., 2024 Dobler et al., , 2026;; Pulvermüller, 2018a).
text.formatted: As a binding device or placeholder, the label links instances that share no common perceptible feature during learning and maintenance, so that a coherent category can form and persist <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Carey, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Dobler et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Dobler et al., , 2026;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Pulvermüller, 2018a)</ref>.

text.text: As a coordination device, the label allows members of a community to align and negotiate meanings (Borghi et al., 2019).
text.formatted: As a coordination device, the label allows members of a community to align and negotiate meanings <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Borghi et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We do not claim the stronger thesis that the label is constitutive of the concept, so that removing the label would remove the concept.

We claim language-dependence, not language-identity: For concepts whose instances lack shared perceptible features, the formation, coherence, and stability of the category depend causally on a label or another stable symbol.
This dependence is graded, varies between concepts, and is empirically testable.
A "label" in this sense need not be a word of a natural language; numerals, notations, and gestures can serve.
Finally, concepts "inside" and "outside" language are not two kinds of thing.

A concept formed largely through linguistic input, such as DEMOCRACY, can be used in nonverbal reasoning, and a concept formed through direct experience, such as HAMMER, can be named, described, and revised through language.
GEST-A describes how much of a given concept's content and organization relies on each source at a given time, not a dichotomy between language-based and experience-based concepts.

text.text: The idea that abstract concepts combine components that are grounded in experience with components that are linguistic, and perhaps components in between, is not new. Harnad's (1990) solution to the symbol grounding problem (how do concepts become meaningful?) is a hybrid of three representations: iconic (analog projections of sensory input), categorical (learned invariance detectors), and symbolic (names and propositions composed from grounded names). Paivio's (1986) dual-coding theory posits both verbal and imagistic systems whose relative contributions differ for abstract and concrete words.

We retain the core of the hybrid view: no single code accounts for all concepts, and the contribution of language grows as the contribution of perceptible instances shrinks.
However, GEST-A differs in four respects.
First, we propose dimensions rather than representational types.
In Harnad's scheme the representational types together make up a symbol-grounding system.
In ours, grounding, embodiment, and situatedness are coordinates that characterize any individual concept at a given time.
Every concept has a position on all three, and the same concept can occupy different positions at different times or in different contexts.
Second, we suggest a decomposed sensory base.
The grounded dimension concerns invariants of the physical world, such as gravity and stable object locations, that constrain what can be learned (Friedrich et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The grounded dimension concerns invariants of the physical world, such as gravity and stable object locations, that constrain what can be learned <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Friedrich et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The embodied dimension concerns body-specific and experience-dependent states, including interoception and culturally shaped motor habits, such as finger counting.
Our use of "embodiment" is therefore narrower than Barsalou's "grounded cognition", which covers all modal re-enactments.
To avoid ambiguity, we use "grounded cognition" for the broader research programme and "embodiment" only for learning-related constraints.
Third, we identify context-dependence or situatedness, rather than linguistic labels, as the most influential cognitive constraint.
Task, social, and formal-system contexts matter, while a label is only one mechanism among several.

Fourth, GEST-A treats being abstract and becoming abstract as two aspects of one dynamic description: It poses both a coordinate system and trajectories through it at the time scales of moment-to-moment context, individual development, and cultural history.
It is sometimes said that abstract concepts challenge embodied cognition because they possess no sensorimotor features (e.g., Mahon & Caramazza, 2008).
text.formatted: It is sometimes said that abstract concepts challenge embodied cognition because they possess no sensorimotor features (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Mahon & Caramazza, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: That statement needs qualification.

If embodied cognition means that every concept is directly and exclusively grounded in modal re-enactment, so that cognition is embodied from top to bottom, then abstract concepts that lack a sensorimotor core do challenge it.
The resolution we propose, that some representations are directly grounded whereas others depend on language and on other grounded concepts, is incompatible with that strong view.
What abstract concepts do not challenge is a hierarchical, systemic version of grounded cognition of the kind that Harnad's (Vincent-Lamarre et al., 2016) hybrid position already allows.
Our claim is therefore that abstract concepts constrain what embodied cognition can mean.
They rule out monolithic accounts and require grounded cognition to be hierarchical and language-inclusive.

Importantly, pursuing a dimensional approach to meaning has a tradition. Osgood et al. (1957) proposed that connotative meaning is organized along evaluation, potency, and activity. Dodds et al. (2026) recently challenged that framework and its successors with large-scale corpus analyses, arguing that meaning is better described by power, danger, and structure.

They also illustrate a more general point, namely that no single axis, including the concrete-abstract continuum, spans conceptual space.

text.text: Grounding constrains embodiment, and embodiment constrains situatedness.
We first describe each dimension and then how they combine.
Grounding concerns the extent to which a concept maintains a connection to observable, physical referents and to the invariant structure of the world (Shepard, 1984; Friedrich et al., 2024).

text.text: Gravity, stable object locations, and object permanence constrain what organisms can perceive.
These constraints are evolutionarily mediated and hierarchically foundational (the "tropic" component of Myachykov et al., 2014).
text.formatted: These constraints are evolutionarily mediated and hierarchically foundational (the "tropic" component of <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Myachykov et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: On the ontological reading of abstractness, DEMOCRACY, LOVE, and ANGER are abstract because they lack bounded physical referents, whereas STONES, BOOKS, and DOGS are concrete.
This corresponds to the philosophical contrast between natural kinds, which exist independently of human observers, and social kinds, which depend on human agreement and institutions (Dunn, 2015).
text.formatted: This corresponds to the philosophical contrast between natural kinds, which exist independently of human observers, and social kinds, which depend on human agreement and institutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Dunn, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: A stone would exist without humans to perceive it; democracy would not.
The connection between a concept and the world it is about (Pezzulo & Castelfranchi, 2007) acts as a hard constraint and a precondition for embodiment.
text.formatted: The connection between a concept and the world it is about <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Pezzulo & Castelfranchi, 2007)</ref> acts as a hard constraint and a precondition for embodiment.

text.text: Two caveats apply.
First, equating ungrounded concepts with social kinds is not fully appropriate.
BLUE is grounded in sensorimotor experience, yet where people draw its boundaries is shaped by social and linguistic factors (Lupyan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: BLUE is grounded in sensorimotor experience, yet where people draw its boundaries is shaped by social and linguistic factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Lupyan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Grounding is therefore one dimension of abstractness and not its whole.

Second, concepts without physical referents plausibly emerged from the need to conceptualize relations that cannot be pointed to in physical space but are crucial for social coordination, such as roles, norms, and moral principles (Borghi et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Second, concepts without physical referents plausibly emerged from the need to conceptualize relations that cannot be pointed to in physical space but are crucial for social coordination, such as roles, norms, and moral principles <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Borghi et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: They are abstract not because they are less real or less important, but because their content cannot be anchored in a bounded physical referent.

Embodiment concerns the body-specific, experience-dependent states associated with a concept: its sensory and motor capacities (Lynott et al., 2020), interoception and emotion (Tallon-Baudry, 2023), and learned cultural practices (Göbel et al., 2011).

text.text: It is contingent on grounded structure, since the body evolved within, and is constrained by, the physical world.
Embodiment can vary independently of grounding.
The planet MARS is ontologically concrete, yet experientially remote, since most people have no direct sensorimotor contact with it.

LOVE, by contrast, is ontologically abstract but experientially rich: most people have embodied experience of loving and being loved, which is reflected in the abundance of similar conceptual metaphors across languages (Kövecses, 2003; Myachykov & Fischer, 2019).

text.text: A concept can therefore be physically real yet experientially remote, or physically abstract yet experientially rich.
The embodiment dimension captures the density and variety of sensorimotor and interoceptive traces associated with a concept, whether or not those traces connect to a bounded physical referent.
Because the traces are modality-specific, embodiment is not a single quantity but a profile across the senses, interoception, and action.

Situatedness concerns how far a concept's content is determined by the context in which it is formed and used, rather than by invariant world constraints or by the body (Robbins & Aydede, 2009; Casper & Artese, 2023).

text.text: Relevant contexts include the task and goal, the social situation, the surrounding discourse, and, for formal concepts, the symbolic system in which they are defined.
Situated constraints are transient, but they shape ongoing processing most strongly, because they serve goal accomplishment (Fischer, 2012 (Fischer, , 2024)).

text.text: Abstractness is therefore not a fixed property but varies with use (Wittgenstein, 1953).

text.text: Two properties of situatedness should be kept apart.
The weight of the situated component is how much of a concept's content is fixed by context of use rather than by world and body.
Its variability is how much that content changes across contexts.
To illustrate, JUSTICE has a high situated weight and high variability, because what counts as just shifts with legal, moral, and interpersonal context.
PRIME NUMBER also has a high situated weight, because its content is fixed entirely by definitions within a formal system, but very low variability, because that system is explicit and stable.
Separating weight from variability removes an apparent paradox, in which precise formal concepts seem at once highly situated and context-free.
Variability can be estimated from corpora with measures of contextual or semantic diversity (Hoffman et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Variability can be estimated from corpora with measures of contextual or semantic diversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Hoffman et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Context-dependence within a single concept is well documented.

The features that come to mind for PIANO differ depending on whether one is imagining moving it or hearing it played, and context-dependent properties are retrieved only in situations that make them relevant (Barsalou, 1982; Yee & Thompson-Schill, 2016).
text.formatted: The features that come to mind for PIANO differ depending on whether one is imagining moving it or hearing it played, and context-dependent properties are retrieved only in situations that make them relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barsalou, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">Yee & Thompson-Schill, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In our terms, the same concept shifts along the embodiment dimension as context changes: it is more embodied in a moving context (weight, grasp, effort) and less so in a context of music theory.
This is different from polysemy, where distinct concepts share a lexical form.
Linguistic context is the most important situating context for abstract concepts.
Distributional learning, that is, learning from the co-occurrence of words with other words, is one mechanism by which linguistic context shapes conceptual content.
We therefore place it within situatedness: it is a route by which the linguistic context of use becomes part of a concept (Andrews et al., 2009; Louwerse, 2011; Lenci, 2018).

text.text: Specificity is not a fourth coordinate of the same kind, because it describes a category's place in an inclusion hierarchy and not the source of its content.
We treat it as an orthogonal descriptor that interacts with the three dimensions.
BANANA and FRUIT share high grounding and embodiment but differ in specificity.
The more general FRUIT subsumes instances with different perceptual features and should therefore tend to evoke more variable simulations.
At the abstract end, FREEDOM OF SPEECH is more specific than FREEDOM and is also more constrained by context.
This generates predictions that cannot be derived from concreteness alone.
The two sub-processes move concepts along different axes: generalization moves a concept up the inclusion hierarchy, whereas detachment moves it through the three-dimensional space.
Some accounts hold that abstract concepts differ from concrete ones in being more emotional (Kousta et al., 2011; Vigliocco et al., 2014).

text.text: Emotional valence explains little variance in concreteness ratings and appears orthogonal to abstractness, not constitutive of it.
The dispute concerns how general the special role of emotion is, not whether emotion matters for some abstract concepts.
We therefore do not list emotion as a separate dimension.

Affective and interoceptive content enters through embodiment, and it varies systematically within abstract subtypes, being strongest for social-emotional concepts and weakest for philosophical-logical ones (Villani et al., 2019), rather than tracking the concrete-to-abstract transition itself.

text.text: In GEST-A the subtypes of abstract concepts occupy different regions within the same space and do not require separate theories.

Their heterogeneity nevertheless has a theoretical consequence: any account of "abstract concepts" must say which subtypes it addresses, since a theory developed around social-emotional concepts may fail for mathematical ones and vice versa.
Feature structure, introduced in Section 6.2, cross-cuts the subtypes.
FEAR, with consistent bodily signatures across instances, differs from JEALOUSY, whose instances vary across social scenarios, although both are socialemotional.
ADDITION with small numbers differs likewise from INFINITY within mathematics.
>Relation to brain-based and simulation accounts
text.formatted: <head n="5." >Relation to brain-based and simulation accounts</head>

text.text: GEST-A is compatible with neurobiological constraints for each of its three dimensions.
For grounding, physical constraints have shaped the sensory capacities, motor constraints, and connectivity of human brains over phylogeny and development (Neubauer et al., 2018).
text.formatted: For grounding, physical constraints have shaped the sensory capacities, motor constraints, and connectivity of human brains over phylogeny and development <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Neubauer et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For embodiment, repeated sensorimotor activity shapes representations through synaptic adjustment (Qin et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For embodiment, repeated sensorimotor activity shapes representations through synaptic adjustment <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Qin et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For situatedness, contextual demands transiently adjust neural processing through attentional mechanisms (Fiebelkorn & Kastner, 2019).
text.formatted: For situatedness, contextual demands transiently adjust neural processing through attentional mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Fiebelkorn & Kastner, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These are plausibility arguments, not tests of GEST-A.
Brain-constrained computational modelling gives a more specific mechanistic account (Pulvermüller, 2013 (Pulvermüller, , 2018a (Pulvermüller, , 2023)).
text.formatted: Brain-constrained computational modelling gives a more specific mechanistic account <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">(Pulvermüller, 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">(Pulvermüller, , 2018a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Pulvermüller, , 2023))</ref>.

text.text: In Pulvermüller's account most concepts lie on a continuum and are held together by features that are shared to different degrees.
Concrete concepts typically show perceptual overlap, in that all instances share defining features.
Many abstract concepts instead show a family-resemblance structure, in which features are shared pairwise but no single feature is common to all instances.
In network simulations this difference leads to distinct learning patterns, and it explains why abstract concepts weight situated components more heavily.
Their representational variability requires linguistic labels as compensatory binding mechanisms for conceptual coherence (Dobler et al., 2024 (Dobler et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: Their representational variability requires linguistic labels as compensatory binding mechanisms for conceptual coherence <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Dobler et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Dobler et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: The results come from simulations constrained by neuroanatomy and neurophysiology, and direct evidence from human learners is more limited; Section 9 states what such evidence would look like.
GEST-A is also compatible with simulation theories (reviewed in Friedrich et al., 2025), most prominently Barsalou's situated simulation theory (Barsalou, 1999 (Barsalou, , 2008)).
text.formatted: GEST-A is also compatible with simulation theories (reviewed in <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Friedrich et al., 2025)</ref>, most prominently Barsalou's situated simulation theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barsalou, 1999</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barsalou, , 2008))</ref>.

text.text: On this view, concepts are not static amodal symbols but dynamic, multimodal representations in the brain's systems for perception, action, and introspection.
Cognitive processing reenacts relevant states in a selective, context-sensitive way.

Simulations for abstract concepts may be more schematic, more reliant on introspective and social content, and more tightly coupled with linguistic forms (Barsalou & Wiemer-Hastings, 2005; Borghi et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Simulations for abstract concepts may be more schematic, more reliant on introspective and social content, and more tightly coupled with linguistic forms <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Barsalou & Wiemer-Hastings, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Borghi et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This theoretical commensurability has several implications: First, simulation is a plausible mechanism for the embodied dimension: for HAMMER it involves motor simulation of grasping and swinging, whereas for DEMOCRACY it involves social scenarios, evaluations, and linguistic contexts.
Second, the context-sensitive tailoring of simulations to current goals is a plausible mechanism for the situated dimension, and it explains why a concept's position shifts with context.
Third, simulation theories agree that highly abstract concepts are multimodal but may draw more on interoceptive and social experience than on object-oriented sensorimotor experience.

JUSTICE may be grounded in simulations of emotional responses to fairness, in memories of social interactions, and in experience of legal discourse, which complements the multiplegrounding view (Borghi et al., 2017; Villani et al., 2019).
text.formatted: JUSTICE may be grounded in simulations of emotional responses to fairness, in memories of social interactions, and in experience of legal discourse, which complements the multiplegrounding view <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Borghi et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Villani et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, simulation theories also acknowledge a role for language: linguistic forms can trigger simulations, constrain them, and provide schematic frames for organizing multimodal experience (Barsalou et al., 2008; Casto et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Finally, simulation theories also acknowledge a role for language: linguistic forms can trigger simulations, constrain them, and provide schematic frames for organizing multimodal experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barsalou et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Casto et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Abstract concepts may therefore rely more heavily on linguistic cues to coordinate complex and heterogeneous simulations.
In Section 4, we described concepts at a point in time.

However, abstraction is the process by which concepts move through the hypothesized 3D space, and it also operates on multiple time scales: Moment to moment, as context shifts a concept's position; over individual development; and over cultural and evolutionary history.
In the sense of detachment, a central feature of becoming abstract is a progressive reduction in the weight of embodied content relative to linguistically mediated and situated content.
We see this as re-weighting and not as loss.
One route to becoming abstract is the gradual removal of properties of individual objects, which yields more general, automated, and simplified concepts.

The process includes generalizing across instances to extract common features, simplifying by discarding irrelevant detail, automating access through familiarity, and categorizing by grouping entities with shared properties.
Generalization lowers specificity.
Displacement is a second route, and it is more directly linked to detachment.

Early communication was plausibly anchored in the here and now, but over evolutionary and developmental time language acquired the capacity to refer to absent entities, past and future times, hypothetical scenarios, and imagined situations (Zwaan, 2014).
text.formatted: Early communication was plausibly anchored in the here and now, but over evolutionary and developmental time language acquired the capacity to refer to absent entities, past and future times, hypothetical scenarios, and imagined situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">(Zwaan, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This progression frees reference from perceptual anchoring.

Reference to present, perceivable entities can draw on rich sensorimotor simulation, whereas reference to displaced or imagined entities relies more heavily on linguistic representation with attenuated embodied content.
Changes in feature structure provide the mechanistic link between being and becoming abstract.
Concrete concepts, and some abstract ones, show complete feature overlap: all instances share features that can be directly experienced.
HAMMER involves grasping, swinging, and striking across all exemplars, so a conceptual system can extract the common sensorimotor pattern through repeated experience.

Many other concepts show family resemblance (Wittgenstein, 1953): DEMOCRACY is instantiated by voting with raised hands, by ballot boxes, and by parliamentary procedure, and no single perceptible or action feature characterizes all of them, yet instances share features pairwise.
text.formatted: Many other concepts show family resemblance <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">(Wittgenstein, 1953)</ref>: DEMOCRACY is instantiated by voting with raised hands, by ballot boxes, and by parliamentary procedure, and no single perceptible or action feature characterizes all of them, yet instances share features pairwise.

text.text: Brain-constrained network simulations indicate that concepts with family-resemblance structure are formed and maintained differently from those with complete overlap.
Verbal symbols support the formation of concrete concepts but are enabling for abstract ones (Pulvermüller, 2018a (Pulvermüller, , 2023;; Dobler et al., 2024 Dobler et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: Verbal symbols support the formation of concrete concepts but are enabling for abstract ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">(Pulvermüller, 2018a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Pulvermüller, , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Dobler et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Dobler et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: The label "democracy" can bind instances that share only partial features into a coherent representation despite the absence of complete overlap.
On this account, becoming abstract often involves a shift from complete overlap towards family resemblance as a concept is applied to more varied instances and contexts.
The conceptual shift connects static and dynamic descriptions.

A concept's position in the 3D space (for example, low embodiment and high situated weight) is the outcome of a history of re-weighting, and feature structure explains why re-weighting requires linguistic binding.
It also implies that feature structure, and not abstractness as such, should predict how much linguistic scaffolding a concept needs.
FEAR, with consistent bodily signatures across instances, requires little; JEALOUSY and JUSTICE, whose instances vary across social scenarios, require more.
A concrete-seeming concept with family-resemblance structure, such as GAME, should show a labelling benefit that its concreteness alone would not predict.
The role of language in this process of conceptual shift needs a precise statement because it is the claim most open to misreading.

The claim defended here is that, for concepts with family-resemblance structure, a label or other stable symbol plays a binding role in learning and maintaining the category, and that its contribution grows as shared perceptible features shrink.
This does not make the label the concept.
There is evidence that labels do bind.

In infants, hearing a novel word applied to a set of objects promotes categorization of those objects (Waxman & Markow, 1995), and in brain-constrained simulations labels improve category formation and persistence (Pulvermüller, 2018a; Dobler et al., 2024 Dobler et al., , 2026)).

text.text: Abstract concepts are acquired late, and their acquisition benefits from explicit labelling and from the situations in which labels are used.
Whether the labelling benefit is disproportionate for family-resemblance concepts, relative to concepts with complete overlap and matched on concreteness, is one of the predictions we make.
There is also evidence that labels are not identical to concepts.

Severely agrammatic patients can retain the ability to reason about exact numbers and to calculate (Varley et al., 2005), which suggests that the grammatical machinery of natural language is not what constitutes number concepts.
text.formatted: Severely agrammatic patients can retain the ability to reason about exact numbers and to calculate <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">(Varley et al., 2005)</ref>, which suggests that the grammatical machinery of natural language is not what constitutes number concepts.

text.text: The symbols that support exact number are not restricted to spoken words: numerals, finger-counting postures and routines, and written notation can all serve (Wasner et al., 2014; Sixtus et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The symbols that support exact number are not restricted to spoken words: numerals, finger-counting postures and routines, and written notation can all serve <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">(Wasner et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Sixtus et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Our term "label" therefore covers any stable symbol that can be attached to a set of instances.
The two accounts of labels as constitutive vs. binding make different predictions.
If labels were constitutive, a concept should be lost when its label is lost, and a label presented without instances should be sufficient to form the concept.

If labels are binding devices, removing the label should degrade category coherence in a graded way while instancebased structure remains partly intact, and a label without instances should not yield a usable concept.
Section 9 states these as separate predictions.
Finally, language is known to influence thought in abstract domains such as time (Boroditsky, 2001) and exact number (Frank et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Finally, language is known to influence thought in abstract domains such as time <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Boroditsky, 2001)</ref> and exact number <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Frank et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Whether such linguistic effects are larger for abstract concepts than for concrete ones has not been tested with matched materials, and we state it as a prediction and not as an established fact.
The account described so far might suggest a single path from rich sensorimotor grounding to linguistic abstraction.
Developmental evidence shows that this is too simple.

Abstract concepts such as JUSTICE are learned late, and one explanation is that they are learned largely from linguistic and distributional regularities, whereas concrete concepts are learned through ostensive links to referents (Sloutsky & Deng, 2019).
text.formatted: Abstract concepts such as JUSTICE are learned late, and one explanation is that they are learned largely from linguistic and distributional regularities, whereas concrete concepts are learned through ostensive links to referents <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Sloutsky & Deng, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Distributional models show that considerable semantic structure can be recovered from word cooccurrence (Lenci, 2018), and early in acquisition words co-occur mainly with their referents, whereas later they increasingly co-occur with other words, a shift in salience from word-to-world to word-to-word associations (Bolognesi, 2020; Louwerse, 2008 Louwerse, , 2011)).
text.formatted: Distributional models show that considerable semantic structure can be recovered from word cooccurrence <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Lenci, 2018)</ref>, and early in acquisition words co-occur mainly with their referents, whereas later they increasingly co-occur with other words, a shift in salience from word-to-world to word-to-word associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bolognesi, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Louwerse, 2008</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Louwerse, , 2011))</ref>.

text.text: For adults, distributional profiles may be stronger than direct word-to-world connections for many concepts, with embodied content remaining accessible but no longer dominant.

Three consequences follow from this proposal: First, for a concept such as JUSTICE the starting point is already situated: it is acquired through language and social interaction and begins with a high situated weight.
Second, such a concept can later move away from abstractness through experience.

Novel concepts learned from language alone can be rapidly mapped onto the body schema (Günther et al., 2020), abstract or socially complex concepts can be represented on a body map that organizes affective and introspective states alongside sensorimotor information (Gatti et al., 2024), and even statistical concepts such as regression to the mean can be grounded through suitable educational experience (Fischer et al., 2022).

text.text: In Stage 1, perceptual grounding, small quantities within the subitizing range (about one to four items) are immediately apprehended and can be embodied in finger counting.
These representations show complete feature overlap: all representations of "three" involve the same quantity and, in a given culture, the same number of fingers.

In Stage 3, relational structuring, the meaning of concepts, such as fractions and negative numbers, depends on their position in a formal system of rules and relationships.

Properties such as divisibility and decomposability are inherently relational and propositional (Shapiro, 1997), and manipulating numbers relies heavily on languagespecific processes (Göbel et al., 2011).

text.text: Both patterns fit the claim that Stages 2 and 3 depend on a symbolic counting system.

Combined with the finding that severely agrammatic patients can still reason about exact numbers and calculate (Varley et al., 2005; Section 6.3), they support language-dependence without language-identity.

text.text: The empirical signature of detachment is a changed distribution of processing and a changed vulnerability to interference.

Meta-analyses of neuroimaging show that concrete and abstract words engage partly different networks: concrete words engage more perceptual and association regions, and abstract words engage more left inferior frontal and anterior temporal, language-related regions (Binder et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Meta-analyses of neuroimaging show that concrete and abstract words engage partly different networks: concrete words engage more perceptual and association regions, and abstract words engage more left inferior frontal and anterior temporal, language-related regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Binder et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Wang et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The contrast in sensorimotor cortex itself is not uniform across studies, and we regard the imaging evidence as suggestive only.

Behaviorally, concrete concept processing is disrupted by concurrent sensorimotor tasks (Scorolli & Borghi, 2007), whereas abstract concept processing is more vulnerable to tasks that compete for linguistic or workingmemory resources (Borghi & Zarcone, 2016; Fini et al., 2022).

text.text: This pattern suggests that abstract concepts depend more on linguistically mediated binding, which is itself a limited resource.
Reduced embodiment does not imply reduced richness or precision.

PRIME NUMBER is extraordinarily precise despite minimal sensorimotor content (Table 2): low in grounding and embodiment, high in situated weight because it is defined within a formal system, and low in variability because that system is stable.
text.formatted: PRIME NUMBER is extraordinarily precise despite minimal sensorimotor content (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>): low in grounding and embodiment, high in situated weight because it is defined within a formal system, and low in variability because that system is stable.

text.text: Its precision derives from definitions and relational position, not from embodied experience, and this combination of minimal sensorimotor footprint and maximal definitional precision is itself a signature of advanced abstraction.
Embodied traces are backgrounded by efficient symbolic routines but not erased.

Finger-based representations influence symbolic number processing in adults across cultures (Dehaene, 2011, pp. 181-183; Domahs et al., 2010; but see Lepoittevin et al., 2025), and latent embodied content can be expected to return under load or in unfamiliar situations.

text.text: A widespread assumption holds that every concept must be directly grounded in sensorimotor experience in order to be meaningful, so that abstract concepts, which lack a bounded and perceivable referent, pose a challenge.
This reading goes beyond Harnad (1990).
text.formatted: This reading goes beyond <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Harnad (1990)</ref>.

text.text: His claim is that the conceptual system as a whole requires grounding, to avoid the infinite regress of symbols defined only by other symbols, not that every individual symbol must be grounded directly.
Analyses of dictionary structure suggest that only a minority of words needs direct grounding, with the remainder learnable from definitions built on grounded words (Vincent-Lamarre et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Analyses of dictionary structure suggest that only a minority of words needs direct grounding, with the remainder learnable from definitions built on grounded words <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Vincent-Lamarre et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The universal grounding assumption nevertheless motivates a research programme that seeks grounding for every abstract concept, typically by correlating abstractness with interoception, emotional valence, or social interaction. Borghi et al. (2017), for example, read the symbol grounding problem as requiring that symbols ultimately be grounded in their world referents, and the challenge of abstract concepts follows from the absence of such referents.

(2017)</ref>, for example, read the symbol grounding problem as requiring that symbols ultimately be grounded in their world referents, and the challenge of abstract concepts follows from the absence of such referents.

text.text: Two levels of analysis are often conflated here: the structural organization of concepts (complete feature overlap versus family resemblance) and the mechanism of semantic reference (direct grounding versus linguistic mediation).

This conflation produces divergent solutions: The systemic solution holds that abstract concepts are coherent because they are linguistically defined in terms of other, ultimately grounded concepts, so that the apparent challenge dissolves (Goldinger et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This conflation produces divergent solutions: The systemic solution holds that abstract concepts are coherent because they are linguistically defined in terms of other, ultimately grounded concepts, so that the apparent challenge dissolves <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Goldinger et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The strong embodiment solution holds that the challenge is real and is met by a richer, distributed grounding in social, emotional, introspective, and linguistic experience, that is, multiple grounding (Borghi et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The strong embodiment solution holds that the challenge is real and is met by a richer, distributed grounding in social, emotional, introspective, and linguistic experience, that is, multiple grounding <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Borghi et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: GEST-A does not force a choice between them.
With respect to organization, it tracks the transition of a concept's dominant mode from sensorimotor to linguistic-relational, which fits the systemic account.
With respect to content, it tracks the transformation of grounding, which fits the multiple-grounding account.
A concept's grounding changes and is re-weighted instead of disappearing, and linguistic binding repurposes embodied content instead of replacing it.
This is a hybrid position, and it does not claim that debates about the best reading of Harnad (1990) are settled.
text.formatted: This is a hybrid position, and it does not claim that debates about the best reading of <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Harnad (1990)</ref> are settled.

text.text: Research on congenitally blind individuals is a critical test case.

Blind individuals develop rich and accurate knowledge of visual attributes that they have never perceived directly, including colors, visual verbs such as "glitter," and animal appearances (Bedny et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019 Kim et al., , 2021)), and this knowledge is predicted by distributional semantics, that is, the statistical structure of word co-occurrence (Lewis et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Blind individuals develop rich and accurate knowledge of visual attributes that they have never perceived directly, including colors, visual verbs such as "glitter," and animal appearances <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bedny et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Kim et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Kim et al., , 2021))</ref>, and this knowledge is predicted by distributional semantics, that is, the statistical structure of word co-occurrence <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Lewis et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The finding does not show that such concepts are purely linguistic, since they are certainly integrated with, and scaffolded by, other grounded modalities such as touch, audition, and social explanation.
It shows that linguistic distributional information can provide a dominant organizing scaffold for conceptual coherence when a primary perceptual modality is missing.
For abstract concepts in sighted individuals the parallel is that, where stable perceptual commonality is absent, labels and their distributional relations can become a primary organizing principle.
The family-resemblance structure of many abstract concepts requires linguistic support for their acquisition, but it does not follow that all abstract concepts lack direct grounding.
Some highly abstract concepts retain complete feature overlap across instances.

CAUSATION, arguably among the most abstract concepts humans have, can be grounded in repeated action-perception sequences such as pushing, pulling, and pressing, which share a common causal structure across all instances (Pulvermüller, 2018b; Wolff, 2007).
text.formatted: CAUSATION, arguably among the most abstract concepts humans have, can be grounded in repeated action-perception sequences such as pushing, pulling, and pressing, which share a common causal structure across all instances <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Pulvermüller, 2018b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Wolff, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Fear, anger, and joy have characteristic bodily signatures (arousal, facial expression, action tendencies), and emotion concepts can be grounded in interoceptive and motor systems (Seth, 2013; Winkielman et al., 2018 Winkielman et al., , 2023)).

text.text: This contrasts with DEMOCRACY or JUSTICE, where instances share features only pairwise and linguistic labels become necessary for coherence (Barsalou & Wiemer-Hastings, 2005; Borghi & Zarcone, 2016).
text.formatted: This contrasts with DEMOCRACY or JUSTICE, where instances share features only pairwise and linguistic labels become necessary for coherence <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Barsalou & Wiemer-Hastings, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Borghi & Zarcone, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The relevant distinction is therefore not between abstract and concrete concepts; it is between concepts with complete overlap, which permit direct grounding, and concepts with family-resemblance structure, which require binding.

A continuum runs from concepts that require substantial linguistic construction (JUSTICE, DEMOCRACY, INFINITY) to concepts that can be grounded directly in repeated action-perception patterns (CAUSATION, FEAR, small numbers), irrespective of their ontological abstractness.
The claim that some abstract concepts are largely linguistic does not deny embodiment.
Language encodes information about perceptual and spatial properties of referents.

The co-occurrence of city names in text mirrors their geographical distances (Louwerse & Zwaan, 2009), linguistic context predicts the perceptual modality of words (Louwerse & Connell, 2011), and word order and co-occurrence carry embodied relations (Louwerse, 2008 (Louwerse, , 2011)).

text.text: On the linguistic shortcut view, language provides efficient access to embodied knowledge without full perceptual simulation (Louwerse, 2018).
text.formatted: On the linguistic shortcut view, language provides efficient access to embodied knowledge without full perceptual simulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Louwerse, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Abstract concepts, built largely from language, thereby inherit indirect connections to embodied experience, even when they lack direct sensorimotor grounding.

This view fits the tradition of treating meaning as use (Wittgenstein, 1953) and the finding that large language models, although trained on text alone, capture substantial regularities in human conceptual structure (Piantadosi & Hill, 2022).
text.formatted: This view fits the tradition of treating meaning as use <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">(Wittgenstein, 1953)</ref> and the finding that large language models, although trained on text alone, capture substantial regularities in human conceptual structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Piantadosi & Hill, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Such findings need not be read as a threat to grounded cognition, since they are what one would expect if linguistic structure encodes embodied information (Winter, 2019).
text.formatted: Such findings need not be read as a threat to grounded cognition, since they are what one would expect if linguistic structure encodes embodied information <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">(Winter, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Our claim here is limited: Text carries embodied regularities.
We do not claim that models trained on text understand language in the way that grounded human learners do (cf.
Chemero, 2023).
To investigate the proposed re-weighting of conceptual dimensions empirically, research has long relied on concreteness ratings.
Large-scale norms such as those of Brysbaert et al. (2014) treat concreteness and abstractness as endpoints of a single bipolar scale and are an invaluable foundation.
text.formatted: Large-scale norms such as those of <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Brysbaert et al. (2014)</ref> treat concreteness and abstractness as endpoints of a single bipolar scale and are an invaluable foundation.

text.text: Methodological critiques nevertheless show that this unidimensional approach has limits, and GEST-A helps to specify them.
The first limit concerns the scale instruction.
The norms of Brysbaert et al. (2014, p. 905) asked participants to rate words from "very abstract (language-based)" to "very concrete (experience-based)."
text.formatted: The norms of <ref type="bibr">Brysbaert et al. (2014, p. 905)</ref> asked participants to rate words from "very abstract (language-based)" to "very concrete (experience-based)."

text.text: This conflates a concept's dominant acquisition modality with its abstractness and risks circularity: if abstract concepts are defined by their dependence on linguistic explanation, finding that they rely on language is a tautology (Lupyan & Winter, 2018).

text.text: Ratings of this kind may capture the very shift from sensorimotor to linguistic dominance that is central to the early stages of detachment (Figure 2).

text.text: The recent specificity norms of Muraki and Pexman (2026) address a different conflation, between abstractness and specificity, and, together with the work of Bolognesi et al. (2020), allow concreteness and specificity to be modelled jointly.

(2020)</ref>, allow concreteness and specificity to be modelled jointly.

text.text: The second limit concerns the concrete pole.
Global concreteness ratings are biased towards visual experience and can overshadow grounding in other modalities.
Modalityspecific strength ratings (for touch, sound, smell) often predict lexical processing better than a single concreteness score (Connell & Lynott, 2012).
text.formatted: Modalityspecific strength ratings (for touch, sound, smell) often predict lexical processing better than a single concreteness score <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Connell & Lynott, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Concepts tied strongly to nonvisual senses (ECHO, PUNGENT) may therefore receive middling concreteness ratings not because they are abstract but because the scale fails to capture their specific sensorimotor features.
Embodiment is multimodal, and its reduction during detachment may proceed differently across perceptual systems.
The third limit concerns polysemy and context.

Treating abstractness as a stable property of a word form is challenged by the fact that decontextualized ratings force participants to average across senses, for example grasping a cup versus grasping an idea (Löhr, 2022).
text.formatted: Treating abstractness as a stable property of a word form is challenged by the fact that decontextualized ratings force participants to average across senses, for example grasping a cup versus grasping an idea <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Löhr, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The word MARS offers a clearer illustration: a rating for the form averages over distinct concepts (planet, God, confectionery), and the same is true of any homonym (Section 2.3).

Abstractness is better regarded as a property of a specific meaning in a specific context, corresponding to a position in the space of Figure 1, than as a lexical tag (Petrova et al., 2018; see also Pollock, 2018; Strik Lievers et al., 2021).

text.text: These observations do not negate the concrete-abstract distinction.
They decompose it.

The classic uni-dimensional scale confounds at least four things: (1) the balance between sensorimotor and linguistic representation, (2) the distribution across perceptual modalities, (3) dependence on context for meaning specification, and (4) specificity.

The empirical signature of detachment, such as reduced sensorimotor engagement or a shift from motor to linguistic interference, is best interpreted as evidence of re-weighting within a multidimensional space.

We recommend that researchers acknowledge the limitations of concreteness ratings, use several operationalizations of abstractness, use sense-level or context-specific materials, include modality-specific and specificity measures, and avoid treating concreteness as the sole or primary dimension of conceptual structure.
A framework earns its place only if it can fail.

If abstraction involves progressive re-weighting from sensorimotor grounding towards linguistic construction, and a transition from complete overlap to family resemblance, then education should ensure strong initial grounding while recognizing that advanced thinking necessarily becomes more symbolic.
The process is a re-weighting and not an erasure, and it generalizes across domains.

In mathematics, effective instruction should progress from situated, experiential representations towards symbolic ones, treating situatedness and embodiment as continuous design dimensions (Chatain et al., 2025).

For concepts lacking complete overlap, including many mathematical, scientific, and philosophical abstractions, explicit verbal labels during learning may be essential and not optional (Pulvermüller, 2018a; Dobler et al., 2024 Dobler et al., , 2026)).

text.text: Moral and legal reasoning offers a related lesson.

Legal judgment retains an interoceptive component even in expert practitioners (Angioletti et al., 2022), which suggests that grounding is a persistent substrate on which instruction should build and not only a scaffold to be discarded.
text.formatted: Legal judgment retains an interoceptive component even in expert practitioners <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Angioletti et al., 2022)</ref>, which suggests that grounding is a persistent substrate on which instruction should build and not only a scaffold to be discarded.

text.text: The pedagogical challenge is to support learners through reweighting while keeping connections to grounded foundations and providing linguistic scaffolding for family-resemblance concepts.
Individual differences in abstract reasoning may partly reflect the efficiency of re-weighting and the capacity to use labels to integrate concepts whose instances overlap only partially.
Abstraction is currently used both as a property of concepts and a process of conceptual development, and a theory of either must first separate abstractness, specificity, and abstraction.

As a property, abstractness is multidimensional: concepts are positioned by grounding, embodiment, and situatedness, with specificity as an orthogonal descriptor, and they vary continuously and not categorically.
As a process, abstraction includes generalization and detachment.
Detachment is marked by a re-weighting of grounded, embodied, and situated content, with a reduction in embodied weight that transforms and does not erase sensorimotor foundations.

Changes in feature structure, from complete overlap to family resemblance, provide the mechanism linking being and becoming abstract, and they explain when concepts need linguistic binding. concepts; they do not constitute them, and the evidence from aphasia, from cross-cultural comparison, and from the diversity of symbol systems that can support exact number is consistent with language-dependence without language-identity.
Abstract concepts do not refute grounded cognition, but they do rule out monolithic accounts in which every concept is directly grounded.
They require grounded cognition to be hierarchical and language-inclusive, and they show the power of language to create conceptual knowledge that exceeds individual sensorimotor experience.
The challenge for cognitive science is not to choose between linguistic and embodied accounts but to understand how they interact to produce the flexibility of human conceptual thought.

20 Hierarchical and dynamic describe two facets of GEST-A. Hierarchical refers to the ordering of constraint: grounding constrains embodiment, which constrains situatedness.

Dynamic refers to how concepts move within the space, synchronically as context changes (situatedness) and diachronically as abstraction re-weights a concept's profile over individual and cultural time.
The hierarchical aspect provides the coordinate system, and the dynamic aspect describes trajectories through it.
Abstractness answers the question "how abstract is this concept?", a measurable property at a given time.Abstraction answers "how did it become abstract?", a process.
Neither reduces to the other: a purely hierarchical description would treat abstractness as static, and a purely dynamic account would lack the vocabulary to say what changes and in which direction.
